extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy, history, and social theory (e.g., Tocqueville scholars and those studying slavery and race relations)
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of slavery and race relations
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter excerpt analyzing the causes, consequences, and future condition of Black and White populations in the United States, with comparative examples (e.g., Ohio vs Kentucky) and economic, legal, social, and demographic arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudice increases as slavery is abolished
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States the prejudices of the Whites against the Blacks seem to increase in proportion as slavery is abolished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation comparing Northern (where slavery abolished) and Southern (where slavery persists) States: although legal slavery recedes, social prejudice remains or grows stronger in freed regions; examples include social ostracism, exclusion from schools, juries, theatres, hospitals, and separate churches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between slavery and its consequences (antiquity vs moderns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate evils of slavery were similar in antiquity and modern times, but consequences differ because ancient slaves often belonged to the same race and could be assimilated after enfranchisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancients could avoid long-term consequences through affranchisement because freedmen resembled born free; modern slavery is joined to permanent physical signs (color), making social reintegration far more difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three post-abolition prejudices to overcome
rubrics_metrics.description: After abolition moderns must contend with: the prejudice of the master, the prejudice of the race, and the prejudice of color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These layered prejudices are 'less easy to attack and far less easy to conquer than the mere fact of servitude.' The text stresses their mutual reinforcement and persistence after legal change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal abolition does not equal social equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Although laws can abolish slavery, manners and public opinion preserve inequality—legal barriers fall but social ones persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: interracial marriage stigmatized, blacks threatened when voting, excluded from juries and many public institutions; even burial practices remain segregated. The text emphasizes the gap between law and social practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free-labor economies are more prosperous than slave-labor economies
rubrics_metrics.description: Provinces without slaves increased in population, wealth, and prosperity more rapidly than those with many negroes; slavery is prejudicial to the master and to regional prosperity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative comparison: Ohio (prohibited slavery) vs Kentucky (admitted slavery) — Ohio more populous, industrious, with shipping, manufactures, canals; Kentucky more sparsely populated and idle. Cited census numbers and infrastructural examples (canal linking Lake Erie to Ohio).

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity and speed: free labor outperforms slave labor
rubrics_metrics.description: The free workman does his work quicker than the slave; rapidity of execution is a key element of economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free laborers work when useful and are paid in money; slaves require perpetual maintenance. The money wages of free workers, though visible as individual enrichment, ultimately return value to the employer via quicker, more economical labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total (hidden) cost of slaves vs visible wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Slave labor appears cheap because wages are not paid directly, but slaves cost the master in ongoing maintenance across life stages, making them ultimately more expensive than hiring free labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintenance costs accumulate 'gradually and in detail' and include food, clothing, care, and support in old age, contrasted with lump-sum wages to free workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural/product suitability: crops and climate determine slavery's economic fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery is naturally more fitted to regions and crops (tobacco, cotton, sugar-cane) that require unremitting attention and continuous labor; corn/wheat regions favor hired seasonal labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rice-grounds and tropical conditions raise special difficulties; southern climate and crop types (especially sugar-cane) make slave labor economically advantageous in the Deep South, whereas corn cultivation favors seasonal hired hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance and social structure influence slavery's persistence
rubrics_metrics.description: Primogeniture and hereditary leisure created an aristocratic class in the South that stigmatized labor and prevented competition with slave labor; abolishing primogeniture produced a class of free laborers and weakened slavery's social base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abolition of primogeniture led to diminished fortunes, necessary labor among formerly idle families, and increased competition between free and slave labor—undermining the master's interest in slavery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition can cause geographical transfer of Black populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Northern statutes prohibiting sale or importation of slaves reduced their market value and incentivized owners to transport slaves to Southern markets; abolition in the North therefore often displaced, rather than freed, slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York examples: prohibiting sale and granting freedom to children born after 1799 made slaves more burdensome possessions and led owners to move them South rather than integrate them locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential demographic and migration effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Free states attract European immigrants and white settlers, increasing white population growth, while black populations (not receiving immigrants) decline proportionally in free states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After abolition, white settlers and emigrants arrive to take up land and labor; blacks, lacking immigration, become a shrinking, often urbanized, underemployed remnant with precarious livelihoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slavery's cultural effect on white character and industry
rubrics_metrics.description: Slave systems cultivate idleness and tastes among whites that devalue industriousness and commercial enterprise; in contrast, free-labor regions cultivate acquisitive industry and versatile occupations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison: Ohio whites become sailors, pioneers, artisans, energetic in pursuit of wealth; Kentucky whites prefer leisure, sports, and military exercises, scorn labor, and thus impede economic development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public health and mortality disparities as indicators of black condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Mortality rates among blacks in free states are notably higher than among whites, sometimes higher than among slaves in slave states, indicating worse living conditions post-abolition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited statistic: between 1820 and 1831 in Philadelphia one white died per 42 individuals while one black died per 21—suggesting harsher outcomes for freed black populations in some northern cities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional exclusion and segregation as persistent consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Even after legal emancipation, blacks are often excluded from civic and social institutions (jury service, shared schools, theatres, hospitals, churches) and face institutional discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text lists concrete arenas of exclusion (schools, theatres, hospitals, jury service, churches) and notes legal rights (e.g., right to sue) are undermined by all-white judges and public prejudice.
